props.title: Food of the Gods II

sections.content: **Food of the Gods II (1989)** (1989) stands as a bizarre entry in the "giant animal horror" subgenre that peaked in the 1970s. Following the loose framework of H.G. Wells' story (like its 1976 predecessor **Food of the Gods**), this sequel shifts the action to a university where growth hormones create murderous giant rats. It fits into the era's trend of environmental horror alongside films like **Prophecy** (1979) and Night of the Lepus (1972), which similarly dealt with mutated creatures. Director Damian Lee embraces pure B-movie excess, delivering outrageous practical effects and deliberately campy performances.

sections.content: The late 1980s saw a resurgence of creature features that mixed environmental messaging with exploitation thrills. **Slugs** (1988) and **The Nest** (1988) followed similar formulas of scientific experiments gone wrong. These films reflected growing anxieties about genetic engineering and chemical contamination while delivering the expected gore and creature effects that drive midnight movie appeal.

Director Damian Lee's approach emphasizes practical effects over plot coherence, following the Roger Corman playbook of prioritizing spectacle. The giant rat sequences, while dated, showcase creative low-budget filmmaking techniques similar to those used in **Killer Klowns from Outer Space** (1988) and **TerrorVision** (1986). The university setting allows for both mad scientist tropes and youth-in-peril scenarios common to 1980s horror. SUBHEAD: Environmental Horror Evolution

sections.content: While **Food of the Gods II** (1989) played its premise for camp value, it followed a tradition of serious ecological horror established by films like **Long Weekend** (1978) and **Frogs** (1972). These earlier works used nature-run-amok scenarios to comment on environmental destruction. The sequel's focus on laboratory experimentation rather than mysterious growth substances reflected the shifting anxieties of its era, when genetic engineering began entering public consciousness.
